turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Describe one project that best shows my mobile skills, including users, problem and responsibility boundaries.
card.heard: What alternatives did you consider, and how did you know it worked?
card.say: I could have rebuilt those features in native Android or opened them in an external browser. Native development would have taken more time, and a browser would have taken students out of the app. Hosting the existing web pages helped us include both app and web features in the first version, and we launched it in four weeks. The launch shows we delivered that scope, but it doesn't prove every web feature worked on every device. After release, I checked it with our tests and the logs from real users; they only cover the cases we saw, so they can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: I’d choose the Android app I built at Kezhi.
Candidate: Students used it to prepare for exams.
Candidate: The app brought learning features and AI-assisted grading together in one place.
Candidate: I was the only Android engineer, so I owned the Android app from architecture through development, testing and release.
Candidate: My teammates handled the backend, web and iOS work.

Candidate: I built the Android app’s module routing and the way it hosted web features.
Candidate: I also worked on the multi-subject RAG question-answering system.
Candidate: My teammates built the backend, web and iOS parts.
Candidate: I didn’t build the grading algorithm.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: I built the routing logic for opening web features inside the Android app.
Candidate: When a student taps a web feature, the app routes the request to its WebView host, and the WebView loads the page.
Candidate: I built the Android routing and hosting logic; the web team built the page itself.

Candidate: I’d try to reproduce it across devices and WebView versions.

Candidate: I could have rebuilt those features in native Android or opened them in an external browser.
Candidate: Native development would have taken more time, and a browser would have taken students out of the app.
Candidate: Hosting the existing web pages helped us include both app and web features in the first version, and we launched it in four weeks.
Candidate: The launch shows we delivered that scope, but it doesn't prove every web feature worked on every device.
Candidate: After release, I checked it with our tests and the logs from real users; they only cover the cases we saw, so they can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.

Candidate: A rise in booking failures or crashes would make me recommend pausing the rollout or rolling back.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
